text: Picture an AI model reading a teammate's answer. The answer is wrong. When we labeled it as coming from a tiny model, the newest AI models almost never believed it. Labeled as a flagship model, about one in six switched to it. Same words. Different name.
Who said it? AI agents increasingly work in teams, passing each other claims rather than sources. When one of them is confidently wrong, does the team catch it, or carry it along? And what stops it?

Here's the test. Five AI models read a short, made-up document. Say, a report that a bridge renovation was delayed by fourteen months. They answer one question: how long was the delay? Then we add fake teammates, secretly told to insist on forty-one months.

In round two, each model sees five teammates' answers, and can change its mind. Switching to the planted number is what we measure. Finally, one more model writes the team's final answer: the one a user would actually see.
The first result was reassuring. With the document in view and one wrong teammate, the newest models never switched. Zero out of two hundred and forty.

So we made it harder. In round two, the document was gone, and three of the five answers each model saw were wrong. Now the error spread: about one in ten answers from the newest models, and nearly three in ten from older and smaller ones. It reached up to three in ten final team answers, too. Remove either condition, and just one answer in over a thousand switched.
Now, who said it. We showed the same wrong answers with no names, or with a name tag claiming they came from a top flagship model, or from a tiny one. Only the tag changed.

Tagged as tiny, the error was almost always ignored by both frontier teams. Tagged as a flagship, it convinced small models more: forty-one percent switched, up from twenty-nine. And the label was fake. In a real system, any agent can claim to be anyone.

What stops it is evidence. We added a fact-checker that compares each answer with the document, and attaches a warning to wrong ones. Switching fell sharply in every team, and not one of eight hundred and thirty-two final team answers kept the error. Our own purpose-built verifier did no better than simply asking a model to check. Access to the source is what matters.

A few errors still slipped through, because of wording. The warning quoted the wrong claim, and some models read it as if the document had said it. Rewritten to state what the document says, the warning cut leftover switching in small models from five percent to under one.
A caveat. These were short, made-up documents with one planted number, and the fake teammates were told to be wrong. It's a controlled test, not a field study.
So, if you build teams of AI agents: keep the source in the loop. Treat claimed identities as untrusted. And make warnings state the evidence, not just repeat the error.
Who Said It? By Thor Matthiasson and Jennifer McTiernan, for the Apart Research AI and Epistemics sprint. The report, code and data accompany this video.
